complexity.notes: Correct but does redundant work: the sort is unnecessary because the index-restricted recursion (each level only looks at nums[i:]) already prevents duplicate combinations, so `needs_sort` and the whole sorting step are dead weight; the extra public `needs_sort` parameter is also an awkward API wart. Each node pays O(n) for the `target in nums` scan, the nums[i:] slice copy, and the [nums[i]] + x concatenation; the standard idiom of passing a start index and mutating one shared path list with append/pop eliminates all of that copying without changing the algorithm. Space figure is recursion stack depth (t/min(nums)) excluding the output list, which is itself exponential.
complexity.summary: Recursive backtracking: sorts the array once, then for each starting index recurses on the suffix nums[i:] with target reduced by nums[i], prepending nums[i] to each returned combination. The `target in nums` membership test catches the single-element completion, and the target<=0 guard prunes overshoot.
